question: I'm really struggling with the "twitchy" front end feel on my 2023 250. The front end feels so twitchy and has a tendency to tuck on corner entry or speed wobble on decel. ... Will 24mm OS triple clamps help?
message_sent: I'm really struggling with the "twitchy" front end feel on my 2023 250. The front end feels so twitchy and has a tendency to tuck on corner entry or speed wobble on decel. ... Will 24mm OS triple clamps help?
rider_context: ~150 lb, intermediate (stated in a later reply); already had suspension revalved by local tech, tried forks flush in the clamps, tried adding more sag; stock springs

response.summary: 24 mm clamps may improve this Honda’s front-end feel, but check the deceleration wobble and front-to-rear balance before buying them.
response.answer:
**Yes—24 mm offset clamps are a reasonable upgrade for this generation, but they aren’t a guaranteed cure for tucking or deceleration wobble.** Several testers found longer-offset clamps improved its feel; twitchiness is a consistently reported complaint on the 2022–2024 chassis.

The important distinction: increasing offset from the reported stock **22 mm to 24 mm reduces trail**—about **2.2 mm**, calculated using a 27° steering angle. It doesn’t add stability by adding trail; the reported improvement is specific to how this chassis responds.

Before spending money:
- Check steering-head and wheel-bearing play, front tire condition/bead seating, wheel true and fork binding. **Don’t ride through a pronounced speed wobble.**
- At your **170 lb geared weight**, establish Honda’s **105 mm rider sag** baseline and measure free sag before changing springs.
- Record fork settings. Honda’s stock baseline is **compression 12 clicks out; rebound 13 out**. Diving under braking suggests insufficient support; getting lower through successive braking bumps suggests rebound packing—opposite fixes.

**My pick:** sort those checks first, then consider the 24 mm clamps if the nervous feel remains; verify the exact OS kit’s fitment for your 2023 CRF250R before buying.

Does the fork dive immediately under braking, or get progressively lower through braking bumps?

question: Bought a 20 at the end of the season ... I now have .46 springs, lowered the oil 20 cc ... the fork compression is out all the way and so is the high speed compression on the shock. Wondered if anyone has any recommendations
message_sent: Bought a 20 at the end of the season ... I now have .46 springs, lowered the oil 20 cc ... the fork compression is out all the way and so is the high speed compression on the shock. Wondered if anyone has any recommendations
rider_context: 175 lb without gear; 67-year-old former vet expert; natural-terrain track, no jumps; .46 fork springs, fork oil lowered 20 cc, shock spring down two sizes, Ride link added; tried stock and RacerX settings; shopping for .44 fork springs

response.summary: Don’t soften it further yet. At 195 lb, your softer fork springs, reduced oil and fully open compression could leave it riding too deep rather than curing harshness.
response.answer:
At **195 lb geared, I wouldn’t soften it further yet**. Your .46 kg/mm fork springs are about 4.5 N/mm—considerably softer than the consistently reported stock fork springs of 5.0 N/mm. You’ve already reduced the oil by 20 cc and opened both compression adjusters, so repeating those changes isn’t the next move.

Testers consistently report harsh stock suspension on this generation, but going too soft can make it ride deep and feel harsh again.

- **If the fork dives and rides deep:** turn fork compression **2 clicks in from fully open**, leaving everything else alone. Retest the same braking section; keep it only if support and comfort improve.
- **If it barely moves and deflects:** check fork alignment and friction before buying softer springs. If it moves freely, a revalve is more useful than opening the clicker farther.
- **Rear:** fully open high-speed compression can sacrifice hold-up. Measure rider and free sag before changing it; **110 mm rider sag** is a commonly reported baseline, not a confirmed Suzuki figure here.

Does it still feel stiff and barely move, or does it dive/squat and get harsh deeper in the travel? That distinction decides which direction to go.

**Changes to try, one at a time:**
- **Fork compression—only if diving and riding deep:** From fully open, turn 2 clicks in.

question: The 2025 Honda crf450 has a hard, spiky feel in the chassis. ... I have been through extremes of adjustment out back (sag from 107-102, clickers from hard to soft etc) ... there almost has to be an uncontrolled wiggle in the frame or maybe the subframe?
message_sent: The 2025 Honda crf450 has a hard, spiky feel in the chassis. ... I have been through extremes of adjustment out back (sag from 107-102, clickers from hard to soft etc) ... there almost has to be an uncontrolled wiggle in the frame or maybe the subframe?
rider_context: Tried rear sag 102-107 mm and clickers from full hard to full soft; harshness felt even riding in the pits; compares to a 2022 KTM 450 SX-F (similar) and a 2025 Yamaha (none)

response.summary: A hard, spiky chassis feel does not by itself point to uncontrolled frame flex. Since broad rear-setting changes haven’t cured it, check for mechanical play or binding before making more adjustments.
response.answer:
**I wouldn’t condemn the frame or subframe yet.** Sharp impact harshness and an actual chassis wiggle are different problems: looseness lets parts move, while binding or excessive damping transfers the hit straight into you.

You’ve already swept sag from **107–102 mm** and tried hard-to-soft rear clickers. That makes another blind rear adjustment a poor next move. A small number of owners report similar rear sharpness on the 2025, but that does not establish a frame defect.

**Next: with the engine off and the bike securely supported, check for play and binding.** Have a helper move the rear wheel vertically and sideways while you watch the wheel bearings, swingarm pivot, linkage and shock mounts; then check the subframe for movement or cracks. Play suggests a loose mounting or worn bearing; sticky movement points toward friction rather than frame flex. Stop riding if anything is loose, cracked or knocking.

For the subframe mounting check, Honda specifies upper bolts **32 N·m (24 ft-lb)** and lower bolts **44 N·m (32 ft-lb)**. Don’t back chassis bolts below specification chasing compliance.

I can guide the bearing checks: tap **Start a guided job**, then choose **Check the swingarm, linkage, steering and wheel bearings**; have a secure stand ready.

Also have Honda confirm whether the 2025–2026 handlebar-clamp recall remedy applies and has been completed.

question: just picked up my first ever KX and want to check/set sag. I'm 185lbs dry, slow vet, for mx only. The ring nuts aren't easily accessible especially with spanners. Anyone familiar with the KX rear shock provide some advice or tips in getting to and adjusting the rings?
message_sent: just picked up my first ever KX and want to check/set sag. I'm 185lbs dry, slow vet, for mx only. The ring nuts aren't easily accessible especially with spanners. Anyone familiar with the KX rear shock provide some advice or tips in getting to and adjusting the rings?
rider_context: 185 lb without gear; slow vet; MX use only on a 2021 KX250XC/KX250X

response.summary: The KX250X preload rings are awkward to reach; unloading the spring helps, but proper hook-wrench access means removing the rear frame and airbox. Measure sag before dismantling anything.
response.answer:
On your **2021 KX250X, proper spanner access means removing the rear frame with the airbox**—there isn’t an easy external preload adjuster. Don’t chew up the rings trying to force a spanner into the gap.

**Measure first:**
1. Rear wheel off the ground: measure from the rear axle to a marked point directly above it.
2. Bike on its wheels: settle the suspension and measure again without you aboard. The difference is static sag.
3. Repeat with you in full gear, standing on the pegs, with a helper balancing the bike. The difference from fully extended is rider sag.

**105 mm rider sag** is a tester-used starting point for this generation, not Kawasaki’s published target. As general guidance, look for roughly **30–40 mm static sag** afterward. Your 185 lb dry weight and saved 205 lb geared weight are consistent; check those measurements before replacing the standard **shock spring 54 N/mm**.

For access, Kawasaki’s procedure removes the seat, side covers, tank, muffler and battery, then disconnects the rear-frame wiring and intake duct before removing the rear frame/airbox. With the spring unloaded, loosen the locknut: turn the adjusting nut **down to add preload/reduce sag**, or **up to remove preload/increase sag**, then lock it firmly.

Kawasaki’s nut-position reference is **123.1 mm**, measured from the upper shock-pivot center; the permitted range is **120.6–132.6 mm**. That dimension isn’t spring length or sag.

I can walk you through **Set the shock spring preload**—tap **Start a guided job** above the message box. Have a stand, hook wrenches, measuring tool and torque wrench ready.

Record your existing settings first. Count outward from gently seated—never force an adjuster—and leave shock high-speed compression where it is until its correct baseline is established. If the suspension is revalved, use that tuner’s baseline instead.

Check free sag after setting rider sag: very little free sag suggests the shock spring is too soft. Springs come before damping adjustments.

message_sent: I can't for the life of me get this bar swapping sensation to go away when I'm on a rough track at high speeds. ... 17 fc350 kyb a kit front forks, bladder conversion on the rear with pro circuit linkage. ... What do you guys suggest?
rider_context: 2017 FC 350 (previous generation, year left null); KYB A-kit forks, rear shock bladder conversion, Pro Circuit linkage; sprung and valved for his weight; fine at Englishtown, worse on harder-base track; short stature; had same issue on a 2015 YZ250F and 2014 CRF250R

response.summary: High-speed bar swapping needs a chassis check before more suspension tuning. Work from your modified suspension’s tuner baseline, not stock FC 350 settings.
response.answer:
**Don’t keep testing it at full speed—bar swapping can turn into a tank-slapper.** First rule out looseness or binding before chasing clickers.

Your Garage lists a 2025 FC 350; you described a **2017 FC 350 with KYB A-kit forks, a rear bladder conversion and Pro Circuit linkage**. I’m answering for that 2017 setup.

1. With the engine off and bike securely supported, check steering-head play and notchiness, wheel-bearing play, loose spokes, tire damage and fork alignment. Don’t tighten the steering bearings to hide the shake.
2. Verify the Pro Circuit linkage matches the bike and shock, and check its bearings move freely. That linkage changes rear ride height and leverage, so stock sag and shock settings aren’t automatically the right baseline.
3. Get the suspension tuner’s baseline for those forks and converted shock, including your weight, spring rates and sag. Start there, one change at a time.

**Does it start under acceleration, or when you roll off/brake?** Once mechanical checks pass: a high, deflecting front under power commonly wants slightly softer fork compression; a diving front under braking commonly wants firmer compression—the opposite fix.

question: I just picked up a 2020 fc250 ... I am 185 pounds ... as i have been getting faster my suspension has just gotten worse ... i also dont know how to set sag on my own. What would you guys recommend
message_sent: I just picked up a 2020 fc250 ... I am 185 pounds ... as i have been getting faster my suspension has just gotten worse ... i also dont know how to set sag on my own. What would you guys recommend
rider_context: 185 lb (180-190); fast beginner, ~2 years riding MX tracks in Texas; stock air fork; adjusts clickers and air pressure without a method; cannot set sag; quoted $1,500 for revalve + spring conversion

response.summary: Start by measuring sag and establishing a known baseline—not buying a revalve. At 185 lb geared, you’re near the top of Husqvarna’s stock shock-spring weight band.
response.answer:
Get the sag and fork air right before chasing clickers. Getting faster loads the suspension harder, so a setup that felt comfortable initially can start diving, riding low or bottoming.

At your saved **185 lb geared**, Husqvarna’s chart calls for a **shock spring 42 N/mm** for 165–187 lb. Don’t automatically replace it: sag will tell us whether it supports you. The stock fork uses air, not a main coil spring.

### Measure sag
You need a stand, tape measure and a helper—a normal tape measure isn’t practical solo.
1. Rear wheel hanging free: measure rear axle to the fender’s SAG mark. Record **A**.
2. Bike upright on its wheels, nobody aboard: measure again, **B**. **A − B = static sag; target 35 mm (1.38 in).**
3. Wearing your gear, sit normally with feet on the pegs, bounce and settle. Have your helper measure **C**. **A − C = rider sag; target 105 mm (4.13 in).**

More shock-spring preload reduces rider sag; less preload increases it. Preload adjustment requires a separate shock-removal job. With rider sag correct, substantially less than 35 mm static sag points toward a spring that’s too soft; the next chart rate is **shock spring 45 N/mm**, listed for 187–209 lb.

### Establish the baseline
Record what’s there first; these are stock-component settings, not a revalve baseline.
- **Sag:** bring rider sag to 105 mm, then check static sag against 35 mm to confirm the spring.
- **Fork air:** establish **10.4 bar (151 psi)** cold, fork fully extended, after bleeding the outer chambers.
- **Clickers:** fork compression/rebound **12/12 clicks out**; shock low-speed compression/rebound **15/15 clicks out**, high-speed compression **1.5 turns out**. Count from lightly seated—never force them.

What does “worse” feel like: diving/bottoming, sharp hits through the bars, or the rear kicking? Until that’s clear, establish this baseline rather than guessing a damping direction. Retest one change at a time over the same section.

For a walkthrough, tap **Start a guided job** above the message box: “Set the suspension back to the standard baseline and check the sag.” Have a fork pump and screwdriver ready too; no parts are needed.

**Changes to try, one at a time:**
- **Rear sag:** Measure first; establish 105 mm rider sag, then check for 35 mm static sag.
- **Fork air pressure:** Record current pressure, then establish the stock baseline of 10.4 bar (151 psi), cold with the fork fully extended.
- **Stock suspension clicker baseline:** After recording current settings, establish fork compression/rebound 12/12 clicks out; shock low-speed compression/rebound 15/15 clicks out and high-speed…

question: on my new 2025 CRF250 ... I have experienced a loss in power and a popping sound when I have blipped the throttle off of a lip. ... if I turn the bike off and try to ride again, the problem seems to go away.
message_sent: on my new 2025 CRF250 ... I have experienced a loss in power and a popping sound when I have blipped the throttle off of a lip. ... if I turn the bike off and try to ride again, the problem seems to go away.
rider_context: New bike; happens late in practice days; after it happens, revving gives pops and bogs; checked spark plug and put dielectric grease on connections

response.summary: HSTC torque control could explain a brief cut when the rear wheel unloads off a lip, but power loss that persists until restarting needs fault diagnosis.
response.answer:
The first thing I’d separate is **traction-control intervention from an actual misfire**. Your 2025 CRF250R’s HSTC watches how quickly engine rpm rises and cuts torque through ignition and fueling. Blipping the throttle as the rear wheel unloads could trigger it, producing a brief stumble or popping sound.

However, HSTC keeps its selected setting after restarting—switching the bike off doesn’t simply turn it off. If the bike stays down on power after landing, don’t dismiss that as normal traction control; an intermittent ignition, fueling or electrical fault becomes more likely.

**First check:** stationary and safely off the track, note the HSTC selection and any PGM-FI warning indication before switching off. Photograph or video any flashes; don’t reproduce the problem over a jump. Persistent cutting or a warning indication on a new bike warrants a Honda dealer fault-code check before further riding.

Does the power return immediately after the lip, or stay reduced on flat ground until you restart? That distinction decides the next test.

Also have Honda check whether the handlebar-clamp recall applies to your VIN and whether the repair is complete; affected, unrepaired bikes should not be ridden.

question: I picked up a 19 rmz250 for cheap ... 34 hours ... Exhaust: .006 L & R. Intake: .002ish L & R. Leak down test: 80% lost. sand sitting top of piston. ... What do the experts of Vital think? Full top end job?

response.answer:
**Yes—budget for a full top-end inspection, including the head, not just a piston and rings.** At a reported 34 hours, sand ingestion matters more than the hour count.

- Your exhaust readings, **.006 in each = 0.152 mm**, and intakes, **about .002 in each = 0.051 mm**, put the intakes suspiciously tight. The exact 2019 clearance specifications aren't confirmed here; both tight intakes can indicate valves wearing into their seats, not simply a need for reshimming.
- **80% leak-down loss is severe if the test was valid.** Incorrect compression-TDC positioning or decompressor interference can distort it. Air at the intake points toward intake valves; exhaust toward exhaust valves; crankcase toward rings/cylinder.
- Sand on the piston suggests intake contamination, although debris introduced during disassembly is another possibility. Inspect the filter seal, cage, boot and clean side of the intake before cleaning away the clues.

**Don't start or crank it with loose sand inside.** Have the head, valves/seats, piston, rings and cylinder inspected and measured; inspect the oil/filter for contamination before deciding whether the bottom end also needs opening. Don't order a piston-only kit yet.

question: Feel like I'm riding a cinder block. It has way too much power down low and none mid-top. It's crazy loose at speed, even with the forks dropped all the way. It reacts like it hit a tank mine to the smallest bumps. ... But what is going on?
message_sent: Feel like I'm riding a cinder block. It has way too much power down low and none mid-top. It's crazy loose at speed, even with the forks dropped all the way. It reacts like it hit a tank mine to the smallest bumps. ... But what is going on?
rider_context: Top AA rider in Florida; forks already dropped all the way in the clamps

response.summary: Some of that matches this Honda’s reported character, but severe instability and violent small-bump reactions need mechanical checks before more geometry or clicker changes.
response.answer:
You’re describing a known weakness of this generation—but **that level of harshness and instability is not something to ride around**. Testers consistently report sharp steering, a tiring chassis on chop and unusually sensitive front-to-rear balance.

The engine complaint partly fits too: several testers found the 2023–2024 motor stronger down low and less frantic on top. That explains the character, not an engine that genuinely stops pulling, bogs or misfires.

**Dropping the forks all the way hasn’t fixed it, so don’t keep chasing fork height.** My order of suspicion is:
- Binding forks, trapped fork air, excessive tire pressure or tight/notchy chassis bearings making little bumps feel enormous.
- Incorrect springs or rear ride height leaving the bike unbalanced; Honda’s standard springs are **fork 5.0 N/mm and shock 56 N/mm**, with **105 mm rider sag** on the standard shock spring.
- Damping that holds the suspension down through successive bumps, or suspension needing service. Honda calls for fork oil replacement every **9 races/about 22.5 hours**, plus after break-in.

Start with the engine off and the bike securely supported: check steering and wheel play, tire pressures, suspension leaks and smooth fork/linkage movement. Don’t loosen chassis fasteners to make it flex.

For the hit, **Mode 2 Smooth** reduces throttle response; it won’t repair missing power.

Has it always ridden this way, or did it start after a service, wheel change or crash? **Stay off fast sections until the instability is resolved.**

question: Now I am early 40's ... Right now Im around 240 but plan on lowering that to 200-210. Not very experienced. ... i've had some say get a 450f of sorts, because of my size. What suggestions do you all have for bikes though.
message_sent: Now I am early 40's ... Right now Im around 240 but plan on lowering that to 200-210. Not very experienced. ... i've had some say get a 450f of sorts, because of my size. What suggestions do you all have for bikes though.
rider_context: Early 40s, ~240 lb (aiming for 200-210), not very experienced; previously rode a stripped KLR off-road; considered a 250 EXC for desert

response.summary: Don’t buy a 450 just because you weigh 240 lb. For a newer rider, manageable power and suspension sprung for your weight matter more than displacement.
response.answer:
**I’d start you on a trail-oriented 250–300 four-stroke, not a 450 motocross bike just because of your size.** At 240 lb, you need suspension matched to your weight—not necessarily more horsepower. A 450’s sharp response can make learning harder and tire you out sooner; being in your early 40s isn’t the deciding factor.

- **Casual trails and learning:** Honda CRF250F. A common beginner choice for manageable power and straightforward ownership; its softer suspension becomes a limitation as your pace increases.
- **Trail riding with room to progress:** Kawasaki KLX300. My pick if you want recreational trail riding and potentially street connections, though it’s heavier than a competition bike.
- **Actual motocross tracks:** Yamaha YZ250F. Better suited to jumps and track pace than those trail bikes, but it’s a competition machine with more demanding maintenance.

Budget for **firmer fork and shock springs** at your current weight, confirmed through sag and travel use. Set it up for 240 now; reassess when you reach 200–210 rather than riding an unsuitable setup while losing weight.

Will you mainly ride trails, motocross tracks, or both? **For casual trails, my starting pick is the CRF250F.**
